o: A straightforward design problem: store tasks globally with sequential ids, keep a mapping user -> task ids, and filter/sort on demand. Due dates are unique, so sorting by due date is deterministic. All bounds are tiny (<= 100 calls, ids <= 100), so linear scans per query are more than fast enough.
k: Store tasks in one global dict keyed by id; per-user lists hold references for quick filtering.
Sort by dueDate on read; completion is just a boolean flag guarded by ownership checks.

a.n: Approach 1: Dictionary of Tasks with Per-User Index
a.i: Global task table plus per-user id lists; each getter filters incomplete tasks and sorts by due date.
s: addTask: assign ++counter id, store {desc, due, tags, done:false}, append id to user's list, return id.
getAllTasks / getTasksForTag: collect the user's unfinished tasks (tag-filtered if needed), sort by dueDate, return descriptions.
completeTask: verify the task exists, belongs to the user, and is unfinished; then set done = true.
a.t: O(U log U) per query where U is the user's task count (tiny under the constraints)

w: The only subtle requirement is completeTask's triple guard (exists, owned, unfinished). Note the C++ ownership check uses the due-date trick awkwardly — a per-user set of ids is cleaner. Follow-up: support due-date updates or deleteTask, which argue for a TreeMap/sorted container per user.
